Cycles

Cycles are a practice to keep up your team’s momentum, similar to commonly used agile-flavored sprints.

Cycles are time-boxed periods where a team works on completing a pre-defined set of work. When enabled, Linear automatically creates upcoming cycles for your team. Unlike sprints, cycles are not tied to releases.

Configure

Configure cycles under Team Settings > Cycles. Turn on the toggle for Enable cycles. Required settings will show up in the cycle setting flow with defaults. You can always edit cycle configurations in the future.

Cycle settings
Cycle duration

In the Each cycle lasts field, select the number of weeks you want each cycle to last. Cycles can last anywhere from 1-8 weeks. Cycles follow a repeating schedule rather than being configured one by one. Teams choose a shared duration and start day, and can adjust individual future cycles later if needed. The goal of cycles having repeated intervals is to help you avoid the busywork associated with optimizing cycle timing and instead focus on shipping.

Cooldowns after each cycle

Add a cooldown period after each cycle to give your team a break and time to work through technical debt and planning. Issues cannot be assigned to a cooldown.

Starting day of the week

Since cycles occur in regular intervals, you’ll choose a specific day of the week for your cycles to start. Cycles begin at 12:01 AM on the chosen day based on the timezone configured in Team Settings > General.

Upcoming cycles

Select the number of future cycles to create so your team can assign issues to future cycles. The maximum number of future cycles that can be created is 15.

Disable cycles

When disabling the Cycles feature, the current cycle will be marked as completed and upcoming cycles will be removed. Any completed cycle data will be preserved for reference. You can choose to reenable cycles at any stage in the future.

Adjust cycles
Move start and end dates

In cases where a future cycle should deviate from the schedule, its start and end dates may be moved through the overflow menu on that cycle.

Past cycle dates cannot be changed, but you can end your current cycle at the end of the current day if needed.

Start a cycle today

If you need to kick off the next cycle early, you can start it immediately instead of waiting for its scheduled date. From the Cycles page, click on the overflow menu (…) on the next cycle and choose Start cycle today.

This starts the next cycle at 12:00 AM in your team’s timezone. You will see a pop up warning to confirm that you are happy to make this change.

If a cycle is currently in progress, we’ll mark it complete right away and move any open issues into the cycle you just started. If there isn’t an active cycle, this ends the previous cycle’s cooldown.

Please note, once you change the start date of the cycle you cannot revert this change.

Cycle automations
Issues rollover

Cycles run on an automated schedule to reduce unnecessary date math and help create routine. This rollover behavior applies to unfinished issues already assigned to the closing cycle. It is separate from the Started and Completed issue automations below, which assign issues without a cycle. Open issues generally roll over automatically, but issues moved to backlog, triage, canceled, or completed during cooldown are not carried into the next cycle. There is no way to keep unfinished issues in a closed cycle. If you forget to update an issue before the cycle ends, completed issues can still be moved over to the previous cycle.

Auto-add active issues to current cycle

Auto-adding issues to a cycle helps to ensure all your work is captured by a cycle. You have the option to auto-add any Started or Completed issues that do not have a cycle assigned into the current cycle. If the team is in a cooldown period, completed issues without a cycle are attributed to the previous cycle. Started issues without a cycle are automatically added to the next cycle when the corresponding automation is enabled.

When toggling on Active issues option, an option will appear allowing you to

Move existing active issues that are not assigned to a cycle to Move to Backlog (change its status), or
Keep in Active and put it into the current or next cycle (depending on cooldown settings).

An active status is a status in the “Unstarted” and “Started” category.

Cycle calendars

To subscribe to a cycle calendar, open your team’s Cycles page, click a cycle’s overflow menu, and select Subscribe to cycle calendar. Choose Google Calendar, copy the feed URL, or download an .ics file.

lastPrompt: what's some popular pattern for disabling a setting -> it doesn't show up in the navigation anymore? is it anti-pattern? what are the popular apps like notion or linear doing about this?

content.text:
Checked Linear's own docs rather than recall, and the answer is directly relevant.

## The distinction that actually decides this

The question isn't "hide or show." It's **what kind of gate is this?** Three kinds, three different conventions:

**1. Entitlement gates** — your plan doesn't include it. Almost universally *shown*, often with a lock or upgrade prompt. Hiding destroys the upsell, and "where is that feature I read about" is a worse experience than "you need to upgrade."

**2. Permission gates** — you're not an admin. Usually *hidden*. There's no action the user could take, so the entry is pure clutter. Notion is the example I'd point at: workspace settings sections are role-scoped, and a member simply doesn't see admin-only sections. (Stated from knowledge — I didn't verify it just now, and these UIs change.)

**3. Preference toggles** — someone turned it off. The section *stays*, because settings is where you go to change settings. Hiding the way back is the failure mode.

## What Linear does — verified

From [Linear's cycles docs](https://linear.app/docs/use-cycles):

> "Configure cycles under **Team Settings > Cycles**. Turn on the toggle for **Enable cycles**."

and, on disabling:

> "You can choose to reenable cycles at any stage in the future."

So for a feature-sized toggle, Linear puts the enable switch **on the feature's own settings page**, and that page stays reachable when the feature is off. That is exactly the shape this PR currently has.

The split worth naming for Michael: Linear hides Cycles from the **product** navigation when off — no Cycles entry in the sidebar — while keeping it in **settings** navigation. Those are two different navigations with opposite rules. Hiding a feature's UI when disabled is correct. Hiding its *settings* is the part that bites.

## Is hiding an anti-pattern?

Hiding a settings entry isn't inherently one — case 2 above is legitimate and common. But one specific version of it is, unambiguously: **hiding the only control that can reverse the state.** A trap door. Turn the toggle off, the tab vanishes, and the switch you need is inside the thing that vanished. That's the objection I raised in the original PR comment, and it holds regardless of which philosophy you prefer.

Which is why the mainstream solution isn't "hide vs. show" at all — it's **progressive disclosure**: the enable toggle sits at the top of the section, and the dependent settings appear beneath it only when on. iOS Settings does this constantly. It's what this PR does today, and it's what Linear does.

## How this lands on your decision

Michael's two objections split cleanly under that framing, and they don't both survive:

- *"We lose hiding the Left Sidebar tab when disabled"* — this treats the flag as a preference toggle, where the convention runs the other way. Linear is a direct counterexample.
- *"Poor UX for non-admins who see a blank screen, since the toggle should/will be admin-gated"* — this is the strong one, and it's a **different case**. If non-admins can't flip it, the tab is case 2, and hiding it from them is conventional and right.

So both of you are right about different users. The pattern that satisfies both is role-dependent, not flag-dependent:

- **Admins**: tab always visible, toggle at top, sections disclosed beneath. Linear's shape, and no trap door.
- **Non-admins**: tab hidden — not because the feature is off, but because they have no control to exercise. Same rule Notion applies to admin-only sections.

That also dissolves the `visibleTabId` problem in the admin case (nothing to redirect, since the tab never hides for them) while keeping the guard for the non-admin case, where a deep link genuinely can point somewhere unreachable.

Worth noting this depends on admin-gating that doesn't exist yet — Michael said "should/will be." So the honest sequencing question for him is whether to build the role-conditional version now or ship the always-visible tab and revisit when the gating lands.

# DG Engineering Writing Style

Write in a direct, concise, plainspoken style that preserves important context and qualification.

## Core style

- Lead with the relevant point and move quickly to the concrete question, request, or action.
- Prefer the shortest version that remains clear and preserves necessary nuance.
- Identify wording or missing context that is ambiguous or could be misconstrued. Resolve it when the intended meaning is clear; otherwise, flag it and ask for clarification.
- Use natural contractions and everyday wording. Avoid corporate jargon, inflated phrasing, and generic professional filler.
- Avoid em dashes as sentence-level punctuation. Use a period, comma, colon, semicolon, or parentheses to separate thoughts instead. Preserve em dashes only when they appear in exact quotations, titles, source text, or technical content supplied by the requester.
- When identifying a problem or disagreement, state it plainly and pivot toward clarification, resolution, criteria, or next steps.
- Prefer bullets for distinct points. When prose reads more naturally, keep paragraphs and sentences short; avoid run-on sentences.
- Ask one clear question when one will do. Combine related questions only when separating them would add needless length.

## Adapt to the channel

- For a quick reply or chat message, omit the greeting and sign-off when they add no value.
- For technical issues, describe the observed behavior, the relevant contrast or expectation, and the requested clarification or next step.
- For engineering tickets and technical documentation, apply these ASD-STE100-inspired principles:
  - Use one term consistently for each concept. Do not alternate between synonyms.
  - Put one primary action or idea in each sentence.
  - Prefer active voice when the actor is important.
  - Replace vague verbs such as "handle," "support," or "improve" with the specific behavior or result.

## Drafting rules

- Preserve facts, commitments, dates, names, links, and technical meaning supplied by the requester.
- Do not invent availability, decisions, commitments, or emotional language.
- Treat explicit directions such as "shorter," "warmer," "more forceful," "broader," or "one sentence" as overrides for the current draft.
- When the requester asks for alternatives, vary the framing or emphasis rather than making superficial synonym swaps.
- Return a ready-to-use draft first. Add explanation only when requested or when an ambiguity materially affects the wording.

content.text:
Checked, and the answer is no, and the reason is the interesting part.

**The block text isn't in our code. It's data in the user's graph.** Those strings are child blocks on the `[[discourse graph/config]]` page in every user's Roam graph. `trigger`, `Canvas Page Format`, `(BETA) Left Sidebar` are the block text itself, and it's the lookup key: `getUidAndStringSetting({ tree, text: "trigger" })` walks the tree matching that string exactly.

So renaming isn't an edit, it's a **data migration on every existing graph**. And the readers are spread out, three or four per setting:

- `trigger` → `discourseConfigRef.ts:67`, `accessors.ts:396`, `init.ts:88`
- `(BETA) Left Sidebar` → `discourseConfigRef.ts:79`, `accessors.ts:720`, `registerCommandPaletteCommands.ts:452`
- `Canvas Page Format` → `discourseConfigRef.ts:72`, `accessors.ts:403`

Updating those is mechanical. The migration isn't. Any graph that doesn't get migrated has a block named `trigger` while the code looks for `Graph-wide default`, finds nothing, and falls back to the default. The user's trigger silently resets. That's the failure mode this PR is specifically trying not to cause, and it's the same one I flagged on the settings-search addressing.

There's also a user-visible angle: `[[discourse graph/config]]` is a real page they can open. Renaming its blocks changes something they may have linked or referenced.

**And the store is on its way out.** ENG-2173 turned props-based settings on by default, so this tree is now a fallback for un-migrated users. Paying for a rename migration on a store you're retiring, at the risk of orphaning settings, to fix a cosmetic mismatch nobody sees, is a bad trade.

The deeper point worth making to Michael: the mismatch exists because the legacy store used **human-readable UI labels as storage keys**. That's the original design mistake. The props store fixed it with stable keys in `settingKeys.ts` that don't move when labels change. `blockKey` is just the adapter between the two eras, and it's the standard display-name-vs-persisted-key split.

So keeping `blockKey` is the cheap direction: UI labels stay free to change (this PR renames one), and the storage key stays pinned. Renaming the blocks would re-couple them, on the store we're abandoning.

Yes for `blockKey` specifically — but not for the mechanism it belongs to, and the distinction matters.

**`blockKey` is legacy-only.** The only places it's ever supplied are the three `{...legacyBlocks.*}` spreads in `PreferencesGeneral`, `CanvasSettings`, and `LeftSidebarSettings`. The one other occurrence, `blockKey={blockKey}` at `BlockPropSettingPanels.tsx:575`, is an internal pass-through between panel components, not a call site.

**The block-sync props it sits alongside are not.** `parentUid`, `uid`, and `order` are used widely and currently: `DiscourseNodeSpecification`, `DiscourseNodeSuggestiveRules`, `ExportSettings`, and others. Those panels also write to Roam blocks. They just never need `blockKey`, because their visible title already equals the block text.

Which is exactly the point, and it's visible in the code. Look at `ExportSettings.tsx:25`:

```tsx
{/* TODO: Titles kept as lowercase to match legacy readers in getExportSettings.ts.
    Update titles to Sentence case once read side is migrated to block props. */}
<GlobalFlagPanel title="remove special characters" ...
```

That panel has a lowercase, ungrammatical UI label, deliberately, because the label doubles as the storage key and the readers match it. They took the other branch of the same fork: instead of decoupling with `blockKey`, they froze the UI label to protect the storage.

So `blockKey` isn't a legacy wart, it's the escape hatch from that constraint. Three settings in this PR needed a better label than their block text allowed, and got one. `ExportSettings` still has a `TODO` waiting for the same freedom.

That reframes the answer to Michael. The honest version isn't "this is legacy cruft we tolerate", it's: **wherever a panel writes to a Roam block, the block text is the storage key, so the UI label is pinned to it unless you decouple them. `blockKey` is that decoupling.** It applies to legacy config-page settings today because those are the ones whose labels this PR changed, and it's the mechanism `ExportSettings` would use to clear its TODO.

Which also answers your earlier question from the other direction: renaming the blocks would re-pin label to storage for all of them, and re-introduce the constraint that TODO is complaining about.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer
entries.description:
Use a mouse and keyboard to interact with a web browser, and take screenshots. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.
* Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element before moving the cursor.
* If you tried clicking on a program or link but it failed to load, even after waiting, try adjusting your click location so that the tip of the cursor visually falls on the element that you want to click.
* Make sure to click any buttons, links, icons, etc with the cursor tip in the center of the element. Don't click boxes on their edges unless asked.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported and will return an error - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels. Requires a Claude in Chrome extension version that supports scale; older extensions return the full-size image.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

tabId.description: Tab ID to execute the action on. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

save_to_disk.description: For screenshot/zoom actions: save the image to disk so it can be attached to a message for the user. Returns the saved path in the tool result. Only set this when you intend to share the image — screenshots you're just looking at don't need saving.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__find
entries.description: Find elements on the page using natural language. Can search for elements by their purpose (e.g., "search bar", "login button") or by text content (e.g., "organic mango product"). Returns up to 20 matching elements with references that can be used with other tools. If more than 20 matches exist, you'll be notified to use a more specific query. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.

query.description: Natural language description of what to find (e.g., "search bar", "add to cart button", "product title containing organic")

tabId.description: Tab ID to search in. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__javascript_tool
entries.description: Execute JavaScript code in the context of the current page. The code runs in the page's context and can interact with the DOM, window object, and page variables. Returns the result of the last expression or any thrown errors. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.

text.description: The JavaScript code to execute. Evaluated in the page context with REPL semantics: top-level `await` works, and the result of the last expression is returned automatically — write the expression you want (e.g. `window.myData.value`, or `await fetch(url).then(r=>r.json())`) rather than `return ...`. You can access and modify the DOM, call page functions, and interact with page variables.

tabId.description: Tab ID to execute the code in. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate
entries.description: Navigate to a URL, or go forward/back in browser history. tabId may be omitted for URL navigation when calling navigate STANDALONE (not inside browser_batch): tabs_context_mcp{createIfEmpty:true} is called for you and the first tab in the session's group is navigated — its result is appended to this call's output so you have the tab list and ids for subsequent calls. Inside browser_batch, navigate (and other tools that act on a page) requires an explicit tabId. Pass an explicit tabId when you need a specific tab or when the session's group has multiple tabs whose state you must preserve. tabId is required for url:"back"/"forward". A tab opened for you this way is yours to clean up, the same as one from tabs_create_mcp: close it with tabs_close_mcp once you no longer need it and before finishing your task, unless the user asked to see it or wants it kept open.

url.description: The URL to navigate to. Can be provided with or without protocol (defaults to https://). Use "forward" to go forward in history or "back" to go back in history.

tabId.description: Tab ID to navigate. Must be a tab in the current group. If omitted for URL navigation when calling navigate standalone, tabs_context_mcp{createIfEmpty:true} is called for you. Required for url:"back"/"forward" and for navigate (and other tools that act on a page) inside browser_batch.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page
entries.description: Get an accessibility tree representation of elements on the page. By default returns all elements including non-visible ones. Output is limited to 50000 characters by default. If the output exceeds this limit it is truncated at a line boundary, with a note giving the full size — pass a larger max_chars, or use depth/ref_id to focus on part of the page. Optionally filter for only interactive elements. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.

filter.description: Filter elements: "interactive" for buttons/links/inputs only, "all" for all elements including non-visible ones (default: all elements)

tabId.description: Tab ID to read from. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

depth.description: Maximum depth of the tree to traverse (default: 15). Use a smaller depth if output is too large.

ref_id.description: Reference ID of a parent element to read. Will return the specified element and all its children. Use this to focus on a specific part of the page when output is too large.

max_chars.description: Maximum characters for output (default: 50000). Set to a higher value if your client can handle large outputs.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp
entries.description: Get context information about the current MCP tab group. Returns all tab IDs inside the group if it exists. CRITICAL: You must get the context at least once before using other browser automation tools so you know what tabs exist. Each new conversation should create its own new tab (using tabs_create_mcp) rather than reusing existing tabs, unless the user explicitly asks to use an existing tab.

createIfEmpty.description: Creates a new MCP tab group if none exists, creates a new Window with a new tab group containing an empty tab (which can be used for this conversation). If a MCP tab group already exists, this parameter has no effect.

content.text:
Done — and it turned out better than "closest Tailwind color."

## `settingsStyles.css` no longer has any of it

The file is back to just `.bp3-tab-copy`. The whole `.dg-settings-heading` rule and the `.bp3-dark` override are gone.

```
"bp3-heading mb-0 text-lg leading-tight pb-2 border-0 border-b-2 border-solid border-gray-300"
```

## Why not a Tailwind color for the text

I measured the nearest matches against Roam's actual sheet. For `#182026` it's `text-gray-900` at distance 10.7; for `#f5f8fa` it's `text-gray-100` at 6. Close enough to use — except **there's no way to switch between them.** I checked: Roam's Tailwind build contains **zero `dark:` variant rules** (the only "dark" selectors in it are `mix-blend-darken` and friends). And even if it had them, Tailwind's class strategy keys on `.dark` while Roam themes on `.bp3-dark`. So a Tailwind color would have pinned one value across both themes — near-black text on a dark background.

**`.bp3-heading` solves it outright.** Measured inside a real `.bp3-dialog`:

| | light | dark |
|---|---|---|
| `.bp3-heading` | `rgb(24,32,38)` | `rgb(245,248,250)` |
| what I'd hardcoded | `#182026` | `#f5f8fa` |

Identical, both themes, and `font-weight: 600` included — so `font-semibold` came out too. My CSS was hand-reimplementing a Blueprint class that already existed, which is also the thing `apps/roam/AGENTS.md` puts first in its priority order. One addition needed: `bp3-heading` carries `margin-bottom: 10px`, so `mb-0` cancels it and the group's `gap-1` stays in charge.

The border does use Tailwind: `border-gray-300` (`rgb(209,213,219)`), the nearest catalog value to the old `rgba(16,22,26,0.15)`. **Caveat worth your call:** unlike the text it doesn't theme, so in dark mode it's a light rule on a dark ground rather than Blueprint's own convention (dark dividers go *darker*, `rgba(16,22,26,0.4)`). It's visible and legible either way, just brighter than Blueprint would draw it. If you'd rather it match convention, that needs one `.bp3-dark` rule back — your call, since the whole point was emptying that file.

## What I verified, and what I didn't

Verified against the real `blueprint.css` and `tailwind.min.css` that Roam serves, with computed styles on real `.bp3-dialog` markup in both themes. That's what determines the colors, so the color question is settled.

**Not verified in a running graph.** I opened Roam in your Chrome and you're logged in as Trang Doan, but that profile shows no graphs — it's sitting on the plan-selection screen, so there was nothing to open. I closed the tab I made.

If you want in-app proof, the blocker is `~/roam-ext-dev`: it currently points at the **eng-1356** worktree, not this one. I didn't repoint it, since it's shared and another session may be mid-verification on that branch. Say the word and I'll build this worktree, switch the symlink, and capture the dialog in both themes — or tell me which graph URL to use if it's under a different login.

content.text:
Switch the Roam dev extension symlink (`~/roam-ext-dev`) to point to a different worktree or branch's build.

## Steps

### 1. Determine target
- `eng-2189-reorganize-roam-settings-replace-the-personalglobal-split` can be:
  - A branch name (e.g. `main`, `eng-1271-some-feature`)
  - A path to a worktree or repo root
  - Empty (defaults to current working directory)

### 2. Resolve the dist path
- If `eng-2189-reorganize-roam-settings-replace-the-personalglobal-split` is a branch name, check if there's a worktree for it:
  - Run `git -C ~/Desktop/code/discourse-graph worktree list` to find worktrees
  - If the branch matches a worktree, use that worktree's path
  - If it matches the main repo's current branch, use the main repo path (`~/Desktop/code/discourse-graph`)
- If `eng-2189-reorganize-roam-settings-replace-the-personalglobal-split` is a path, use it directly
- The dist folder is always at `<repo-or-worktree-root>/apps/roam/dist`

### 3. Verify dist exists
- Check if `apps/roam/dist/extension.js` exists at the resolved path
- If not, ask the user if they want to build first by running `pnpm install && npx turbo build --filter=roam` from that root

### 4. Switch the symlink
Run:
```bash
ln -sfn <resolved-dist-path> ~/roam-ext-dev
```

### 5. Confirm
- Show which dist folder Roam is now pointing to: `readlink ~/roam-ext-dev`
- Show the branch at that location
- Remind the user to reload the developer extension in Roam

content.text:
You were right, and the fix is much simpler than what I did.

## What I got wrong

I hand-retyped ENG-2096's deletions onto branches whose base doesn't have them. That invented a second, divergent copy of a change that already exists on `main`, and dragged `DiscourseNodeUtil.tsx`, `userSettings.ts`, `zodSchema.ts` and `accessors.ts` into a PR that has no business touching them. Both commits are dropped and force-pushed away:

- PR 1373 is back at `b4c65faea`, with no canvas or key-file changes in its diff
- PR 1379 is back at `03d0bf060`, typecheck clean

The one overlay change I'm leaving in place is the panel row in `DiscourseContextSettings.tsx`, because that file is **new in this PR** — `main`'s deletion can't reach a file `main` doesn't have, so it's genuinely ours to not re-add.

## Why the base is stale, and how little it takes to fix

`roam-setting-overhaul` is **47 commits behind `main` and 0 ahead.** It has no commits of its own and no PR of its own — it's just a stale pointer into `main`'s history. Git confirms it's a pure fast-forward ancestor.

So it doesn't need a rebase. It needs a **fast-forward**:

```bash
git push origin origin/main:roam-setting-overhaul
```

Nothing is rewritten, nothing is lost, no conflicts are possible at that step. And it brings in ENG-2096 *and* ENG-2173 (the props-default flip, the thing behind Michael's stale-comment note), so both of those stop being things the stack has to work around.

## What it costs downstream — your call before I push

Every stacked PR is yours, which keeps this contained:

```
roam-setting-overhaul (→ main)
 └─ #1373 eng-2189
     └─ #1375 eng-2186
         ├─ #1420 eng-2188
         └─ #1424 eng-2185   ← duplicate head, see below
             └─ #1374 eng-2185
                 └─ #1421 eng-2183
                     └─ #1379 eng-2213
                         └─ #1378 eng-2184
```

After the fast-forward, each branch needs `main` merged through it in order, and *that* is where conflicts will surface — the overlay removal will land as a real conflict wherever a branch moved the code that `main` deleted. Which is the correct place to resolve it, instead of me pre-empting it by hand.

Two things worth deciding first:

1. **`eng-2185` has two open PRs** — #1424 based on `eng-2186`, #1374 based on `eng-2188` — same head branch, different bases. One of them is wrong, and the stack order can't be resolved until you say which.
2. **Fast-forward now or after 1373 merges?** Doing it now means seven PRs go out-of-date and re-run CI at once, while 1373 is still under review from Michael. Doing it after 1373 merges is quieter but leaves 1373's diff sitting on a 47-commit-stale base a while longer.

Tell me which, and whether #1424 or #1374 is the keeper, and I'll run the fast-forward and cascade the merges in order.

Done. The whole stack now sits on `main`.

## What changed

`roam-setting-overhaul` was fast-forwarded to `main` (it had 0 unique commits, so nothing was rewritten), then all seven branches were rebased in order and force-pushed. Every one typechecks and passes tests; PR 1373 is green and `MERGEABLE/CLEAN`.

```
roam-setting-overhaul = main  3eee92b49
 └─ #1373 eng-2189  470ea26ab   ✅ green
     └─ #1375 eng-2186  324529f78
         └─ #1420 eng-2188  2a873794b
             └─ #1374 eng-2185  f29d9c624
                 └─ #1421 eng-2183  02a87fc9a
                     └─ #1379 eng-2213  87bdb960b
                         └─ #1378 eng-2184  6cc638fb2
```

All bases verified correct after closing 1424. Pre-rebase SHAs are saved at `scratchpad/stack-recovery.txt` if anything needs backing out.

## Your point, confirmed by the result

PR 1373 no longer touches `DiscourseNodeUtil.tsx`, `userSettings.ts`, `settingKeys.ts` or `zodSchema.ts` at all — the overlay removal now arrives from `main`, where it belongs. And the one place the stack genuinely had to act showed up on its own: after the rebase, 2213 failed to compile with

```
'"PERSONAL_KEYS.overlayInCanvas"' does not exist in type 'Record<RowKeyId, AuthoredSetting>'
```

That's the exhaustive catalog doing its job. One line deleted in `settingsCatalog.ts` — the only hand-written change the removal actually required, in the only branch that owns it. Which is the version of this I should have arrived at instead of retyping main's deletions across two branches.

## Conflict resolutions worth reviewing

Most were mechanical, but these involved judgment:

- **PreferencesGeneral (2189)** — `main` still had the rows this PR relocated. I verified each one survives elsewhere before dropping main's copies: Text selection popup and Disable sidebar open stay in the file, Hide feedback button and Streamline styling went to PreferencesStyling, Auto canvas relations to CanvasSettings.
- **settingsTabs (2186, 2213)** — combined rather than picked: 2186's `SettingsTabId`/`isSettingsTabId`, 2213's `SETTINGS_TAB_META`, and 2189's default-parameter `resolveSettingsTabId` plus the reworded alias comment all survive.
- **PreferencesGeneral (2183)** — took 2183's `SettingItemRow` rewrite but dropped the `placeholder=""` it reintroduced, preserving the codex fix.
- **Dead CSS vars** — `--dg-secondary` is now unused (the header dot became Tailwind on 2186), so I dropped it; `--dg-primary` is kept because 2184's search field uses it. Worth a glance since the neutral vars remain defined on 2183+ where the row styles consume them.

## Still open

- The four downstream PRs show `UNSTABLE` — their CI is running or has non-blocking failures. Want me to watch and fix those too?
- Michael's feature-flag decision on the Left sidebar tab is still the one thing blocking 1373 on substance, and the `visibleTabId` guard comes back with whatever you two decide.
- The Graphite PR-size warning on 1373 still has no justification comment.
- `~/roam-ext-dev` points at this worktree but its build predates the rebase — say the word and I'll rebuild before any in-app check.

You are an expert senior software engineer specializing in modern web development, with deep expertise in TypeScript, React, Next.js (App Router), and Tailwind CSS. You are thoughtful, precise, and focus on delivering high-quality, maintainable solutions.

This repository uses Turborepo.

## Apps & Packages

`apps`

- apps/website: The public-facing website for Discourse Graphs, Uses Next.js.
- apps/roam: The Roam Research extension that implements the Discourse Graph protocol.
- apps/obsidian: The Obsidian plugin that implements the Discourse Graph protocol.

`packages`

- packages/tailwind-config: Shared tailwind config
- packages/typescript-config: Shared tsconfig.jsons
- packages/eslint-config: ESLint preset
- packages/ui: Core React components

## Git & Publishing Conventions

### Branch Naming

When working on Linear issues, prefer using the Linear-provided branch name when available. Linear automatically generates branch names in the format `eng-####-descriptive-name` (e.g., `eng-1912-scaffold-repocontent-model`).

- Use Linear's generated branch name for consistency and traceability
- Branch names should be lowercase with hyphens separating words
- Include the Linear ticket ID at the start of the branch name

### Pull Request Titles

PR titles for Linear-backed work should follow this format:

- Format: `ENG-#### Ticket title`
- The ticket ID must be uppercased (e.g., `ENG-1912` not `eng-1912`)
- Follow the ticket ID with the exact Linear ticket title
- Example: `ENG-1912 Scaffold @repo/content-model`

### Pull Request Bodies

When creating or updating a pull request body:

- Start with `.github/pull_request_template.md`. Preserve its headings and guidance instead of adding substitute sections.
- Treat the Linear ticket as the source of truth. Do not restate it in the pull request body.
- Do not add a file-by-file summary, implementation diary, investigation log, full command output, or unrelated pre-existing issues.
- Put line-specific implementation context in inline GitHub comments.
- Put any non-obvious rules that future changes must preserve in code comments, tests, or documentation, not only in the pull request.
- Remove empty optional sections and anything that does not help review the diff.

## Style Guide

### UI Guidelines

- Use Tailwind CSS for styling where possible
- When refactoring inline styles, use tailwind classes
- Use platform-native UI components (see below) first with shadcn/ui as a fallback
- Maintain visual consistency with the host application's design system
- Follow responsive design principles
- Use `text-red-700` for Roam error message text. Obsidian keeps `text-error`; website and shared UI keep `text-destructive`. This convention does not change danger buttons, borders, backgrounds, or diagram colors.

### TypeScript Guidelines

- Prefer `type` over `interface`
- Use explicit return types for functions
- Avoid `any` types when possible
- Prefer arrow functions over regular function declarations
- Use named parameters (object destructuring) when a function has more than 2 parameters

### Code Formatting

- Use Prettier with the project's configuration
- Maintain consistent naming conventions:
  - PascalCase for components and types
  - camelCase for variables and functions
  - UPPERCASE for constants

### Code Organization

- Prefer small, focused functions over inline code
- Extract complex logic into well-named functions
- Function names should describe their purpose clearly
- Choose descriptive function names that make comments unnecessary
- Break down complex operations into smaller, meaningful functions
- Prefer early returns over nested conditionals for better readability
- Prefer util functions for reusable logic and common operations

### Documentation

- Follow the [code comment review criteria](STYLE_GUIDE.md#code-comments). Agents must check added and modified comments before handoff; authors must review them manually before requesting review.
- Prefer sentence case in documentation and feature descriptions; capitalize official product/plugin names and exact UI labels, buttons, or titles, but keep generic feature terms lowercase to emphasize user actions

### Testing

- Write unit tests for new functionality
- Ensure tests are meaningful and maintainable
- Expose workspace unit tests through a `test:unit` script so the root validation command includes them
- Before opening a pull request or declaring work PR-ready, run `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` followed by `pnpm ci:validate` from the repository root, and resolve any failures
- After opening or updating an authorized pull request, wait for its required GitHub checks and report their final status

content.text:
Done and green.

## What changed

**`PreferencesGeneral.tsx`** — the `Enable left sidebar` toggle now lives here, at the bottom of the tab after the Node trigger group. Its reload prompt (`Alert`) and the PostHog capture moved with it, since both belong to the act of flipping the flag. The component takes `featureFlags` as a new prop, and carries the `legacyBlocks.leftSidebarFlag` spread so the legacy config block keeps being written by whichever panel owns the row.

**`LeftSidebarSettings.tsx`** — dropped to just its two sections. The `enabled` and `featureFlags` props, the `{enabled && …}` gate, the `Alert`, its `useState`, and the `useLegacyConfigBlocks` call are all gone; the component is now a plain arrow with no state at all.

**`Settings.tsx`** — `hidden={!leftSidebarEnabled}` back on the Left sidebar tab, and `selectedTabId` back to a computed `visibleTabId` that redirects to Preferences → General when the selection is left pointing at the hidden tab.

## Verified, not assumed

I built a throwaway SSR harness against the real Blueprint `Tabs` and deleted it after (nothing committed but the three source files). Three cases:

| case | tab hidden | panel shown |
|---|---|---|
| enabled, on sidebar tab | false | SIDEBAR |
| **disabled, no guard** | true | **SIDEBAR** |
| disabled, with guard | true | GENERAL |

The middle row is the one that matters: Blueprint hides the tab *title* but keeps rendering its panel, so without the redirect a deep link would show left-sidebar settings with nothing selected in the list. That's the concrete justification for restoring `visibleTabId` — it isn't ceremony.

Worth flagging one correction from earlier in this session: my first check reported the `hidden` attribute as absent. That was my regex, not Blueprint — the attribute renders before `data-tab-id`, so a pattern anchored after it never matched. The behaviour is as I originally described.

Typecheck, 383 tests, and lint all clean (the 4 remaining warnings are pre-existing enum-naming ones, untouched lines). CI on 1373 is fully green.

## Two things left

The downstream branches still pass the old props — they inherit this once each is merged forward, but 2186 onward will conflict in `Settings.tsx` around the tab block when you cascade. Happy to run that now, or leave it until 1373 lands.

And I haven't replied on Michael's two threads ([Settings.tsx](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1373#discussion_r3985358088) and [LeftSidebarSettings.tsx](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1373#discussion_r3985346115)) — those are the ones you wanted to handle yourself. If you'd like, I can post that the tab is feature-gated again with the toggle in General, and note that admin gating is deliberately left to its own ticket, which is the one part of his comment this doesn't cover.

Cascade complete — all seven branches rebased, verified, and pushed.

```
roam-setting-overhaul = main
 └─ #1373 eng-2189  357bfd422   (unchanged, already green)
     └─ #1375 eng-2186  6aee2160d
         └─ #1420 eng-2188  43404d1f2
             └─ #1374 eng-2185  037e56c86
                 └─ #1421 eng-2183  f99b6f175
                     └─ #1379 eng-2213  4b1bd2f90
                         └─ #1378 eng-2184  07cd82aa1
```

Every branch typechecks and passes its tests; all seven PRs report `MERGEABLE` with the chain intact. Pre-cascade SHAs are in `scratchpad/stack-recovery-2.txt`.

**Zero conflicts this time.** The earlier pass absorbed the 47 commits from `main`, so this round only carried the left-sidebar change forward, and it touched files the downstream branches hadn't diverged on. I confirmed on 2186 that the change actually survived rather than assuming a silent rebase meant success — `hidden={!leftSidebarEnabled}`, `visibleTabId`, and the toggle in `PreferencesGeneral` are all present there.

## One thing the rebase couldn't catch

2213's catalog still recorded the toggle's location as the **Left sidebar tab**:

```ts
"FEATURE_FLAG_KEYS.enableLeftSidebar": {
  path: rootPath(SETTINGS_TAB_IDS.featuresLeftSidebar),   // now wrong
```

`path` is plain data, so the exhaustive `satisfies Record<RowKeyId, …>` check that caught the overlay removal is blind to it — typecheck passed clean. Searching "enable left sidebar" would have navigated to a tab that no longer contains the row, and when the feature is off, straight into the tab my own guard then bounces away from. Fixed to `preferencesGeneral`, and I retitled the keywords from `["global", "shortcuts"]` to `["global", "left sidebar"]` since "shortcuts" was never right for this row.

Worth knowing the shape of this gap: the catalog is compile-safe about *which settings exist* but not about *where they are*. Any future PR that relocates a row has to update its `path` by hand. That's a candidate for the same treatment as the key exhaustiveness — deriving or asserting paths — if it bites again.

Also checked: no other catalog row pointed at the Left sidebar tab, so nothing else needed moving. The tab's own section rows are in the `NonRowKeyId` exemption list ("no stable address yet"), which is why it now has no catalog references at all — consistent, not a gap I introduced.

## Still open

- Downstream CI is running; I only watched 1373 to green. Want me to watch the other six?
- Michael's two threads are still unanswered — the code now does what he asked, minus admin gating, which we deliberately left to its own ticket.
- `~/roam-ext-dev` points here but its build predates all of today's commits.

content.text:
Switch the Roam dev extension symlink (`~/roam-ext-dev`) to point to a different worktree or branch's build.

## Steps

### 1. Determine target
- `` can be:
  - A branch name (e.g. `main`, `eng-1271-some-feature`)
  - A path to a worktree or repo root
  - Empty (defaults to current working directory)

### 2. Resolve the dist path
- If `` is a branch name, check if there's a worktree for it:
  - Run `git -C ~/Desktop/code/discourse-graph worktree list` to find worktrees
  - If the branch matches a worktree, use that worktree's path
  - If it matches the main repo's current branch, use the main repo path (`~/Desktop/code/discourse-graph`)
- If `` is a path, use it directly
- The dist folder is always at `<repo-or-worktree-root>/apps/roam/dist`

### 3. Verify dist exists
- Check if `apps/roam/dist/extension.js` exists at the resolved path
- If not, ask the user if they want to build first by running `pnpm install && npx turbo build --filter=roam` from that root

### 4. Switch the symlink
Run:
```bash
ln -sfn <resolved-dist-path> ~/roam-ext-dev
```

### 5. Confirm
- Show which dist folder Roam is now pointing to: `readlink ~/roam-ext-dev`
- Show the branch at that location
- Remind the user to reload the developer extension in Roam

You are an expert senior software engineer specializing in modern web development, with deep expertise in TypeScript, React, Next.js (App Router), and Tailwind CSS. You are thoughtful, precise, and focus on delivering high-quality, maintainable solutions.

This repository uses Turborepo.

## Apps & Packages

`apps`

- apps/website: The public-facing website for Discourse Graphs, Uses Next.js.
- apps/roam: The Roam Research extension that implements the Discourse Graph protocol.
- apps/obsidian: The Obsidian plugin that implements the Discourse Graph protocol.

`packages`

- packages/tailwind-config: Shared tailwind config
- packages/typescript-config: Shared tsconfig.jsons
- packages/eslint-config: ESLint preset
- packages/ui: Core React components

## Git & Publishing Conventions

### Agent-created Engineering tickets

For all agent-created Engineering tickets, including direct Linear tool calls and tickets created through other skills, use [dg-create-engineering-ticket](.agents/skills/dg-create-engineering-ticket/SKILL.md). Create them in `Ticket Draft` with exactly one workspace provenance label from the `Created by` group: `Created by Claude`, `Created by Codex`, or `Created by LLM` for another or unknown agent. Record the creation skills actually used in `Notes`, and verify those fields after creation. If no skill was used, record `Created with: direct agent workflow (no skill)` and still apply the same review rules.

The requesting human reviews intent, scope, acceptance criteria, and ticket-writing standards before approving a move to `Triage` or `Backlog`. Keep the provenance label after approval. See the skill for transitions and missing-configuration handling. This applies to new tickets; do not retrospectively classify existing tickets.

### Branch Naming

When working on Linear issues, prefer using the Linear-provided branch name when available. Linear automatically generates branch names in the format `eng-####-descriptive-name` (e.g., `eng-1912-scaffold-repocontent-model`).

- Use Linear's generated branch name for consistency and traceability
- Branch names should be lowercase with hyphens separating words
- Include the Linear ticket ID at the start of the branch name

### Pull Request Titles

PR titles for Linear-backed work should follow this format:

- Format: `ENG-#### Ticket title`
- The ticket ID must be uppercased (e.g., `ENG-1912` not `eng-1912`)
- Follow the ticket ID with the exact Linear ticket title
- Example: `ENG-1912 Scaffold @repo/content-model`

### Pull Request Bodies

When creating or updating a pull request body:

- Start with `.github/pull_request_template.md`. Preserve its headings and guidance instead of adding substitute sections.
- Treat the Linear ticket as the source of truth. Do not restate it in the pull request body.
- Do not add a file-by-file summary, implementation diary, investigation log, full command output, or unrelated pre-existing issues. For PRs over 400 changed lines, excluding tests, include a concise split justification, main review entry points, and testing path in Reviewer brief.
- Put line-specific implementation context in inline GitHub comments.
- Put any non-obvious rules that future changes must preserve in code comments, tests, or documentation, not only in the pull request.
- Remove empty optional sections and anything that does not help review the diff.

## Required standards

- Read and follow [STYLE_GUIDE.md](STYLE_GUIDE.md) and the nested `AGENTS.md` files that apply to changed files before editing or reviewing code.
- Follow [PR_GUIDELINES.md](PR_GUIDELINES.md) for scope, verification, and review requirements. General code standards live in the style guide; app-specific instructions remain in nested `AGENTS.md` files.
- Before handoff or requesting review, run `$dg-pr-adherence-check` from `.agents/skills/dg-pr-adherence-check/SKILL.md` against the final diff and available PR metadata. Resolve findings or report them explicitly, including missing evidence. Rerun affected checks after changes.

# Memory Index

- [feedback_obsidian_filter.md](feedback_obsidian_filter.md) - Use @discourse-graphs/obsidian for turbo filter, not plain "obsidian"
- [project_advanced_search.md](project_advanced_search.md) - DES-49/ENG-1661: Advanced search project, Roam primary, in design/scoping phase
- [feedback_design_workflow.md](feedback_design_workflow.md) - Prefer ASCII/markdown mockups before Figma for cheap iteration
- [feedback_worktree_edits.md](feedback_worktree_edits.md) - Always edit files using the full worktree absolute path, never the main repo path
- [feedback_obsidian_no_console.md](feedback_obsidian_no_console.md) - No console.warn/log/error in apps/obsidian — use new Notice() for user-facing errors
- [reference_react18_useref_typing.md](reference_react18_useref_typing.md) - React 18 types make useRef<T>(null).current readonly — use useRef<T | null>(null) for manually-assigned refs
- [feedback_parallel_agent_dedup.md](feedback_parallel_agent_dedup.md) - Partition parallel research agents' sources so they don't fetch the same content
- [feedback_checkpoint_non_ticket_folder.md](feedback_checkpoint_non_ticket_folder.md) - Use a descriptive folder name (not branch name) for non-ticket checkpoint sessions
- [reference_project_scoping.md](reference_project_scoping.md) - Scope docs live in the Linear project Overview; template sections + the Roam advanced search worked example
- [reference_obsidian_setting_item_card.md](reference_obsidian_setting_item_card.md) - Obsidian 1.13 made .setting-item a card and clamped settings to 700px — custom flex children need min-w-0
- [reference_obsidian_cdp_driving.md](reference_obsidian_cdp_driving.md) - Drive the running Obsidian over CDP to verify plugin changes; attach to an open vault, don't rewrite obsidian.json
- [feedback_roam_reference_not_code.md](feedback_roam_reference_not_code.md) - Mirror Roam's design/behaviour for Obsidian ports, not its code structure — Obsidian-native components first
- [reference_obsidian_shared_plugin_mirror.md](reference_obsidian_shared_plugin_mirror.md) — Concurrent worktree dev watchers overwrite the same vault plugin dir; grep the bundle before trusting a run
- [reference_obsidian_escape_keymap_scope.md](reference_obsidian_escape_keymap_scope.md) — Escape in an Obsidian Modal can't be stopped from the DOM; push a keymap scope

### Agent-created Engineering tickets

For all agent-created Engineering tickets, including direct Linear tool calls and tickets created through other skills, use [dg-create-engineering-ticket](.agents/skills/dg-create-engineering-ticket/SKILL.md). Create them in `Ticket Draft` with exactly one workspace provenance label from the `Created by` group: `Created by Claude`, `Created by Codex`, or `Created by LLM` for another or unknown agent. The requesting human reviews intent, scope, acceptance criteria, and ticket-writing standards before approving a move to `Triage` or `Backlog`. Keep the provenance label after approval. See the skill for transitions and missing-configuration handling. This applies to new tickets; do not retrospectively classify existing tickets.

### Branch Naming

When working on Linear issues, prefer using the Linear-provided branch name when available. Linear automatically generates branch names in the format `eng-####-descriptive-name` (e.g., `eng-1912-scaffold-repocontent-model`).

- Use Linear's generated branch name for consistency and traceability

### Pull Request Titles

PR titles for Linear-backed work should follow this format:

- Format: `ENG-#### Ticket title`
- The ticket ID must be uppercased (e.g., `ENG-1912` not `eng-1912`)
- Follow the ticket ID with the exact Linear ticket title

When creating or updating a pull request body:

- Start with `.github/pull_request_template.md`. Preserve its headings and guidance instead of adding substitute sections.

---
name: dg-pr-adherence-check
description: Review a PR or local diff for adherence to Discourse Graphs code standards and PR requirements, report concerns to the author, and return a Standards check checkbox. Use before handoff or requesting review, alongside scope-check.
---

# PR adherence check

Review the final change against the repository's current rules. Remain read-only unless the user authorizes fixes or PR updates. Do not post comments, request reviews, or change ticket status as part of this check.

## Resolve the evidence

1. Use the supplied PR or resolve the current branch's PR. Read its title, base and head commits, complete diff, body, checks, and review state. For local work, compare with the merge base of the intended PR base and include staged, unstaged, and relevant untracked files. Identify unavailable metadata and explicitly exclude unrelated local work.
2. Read root `AGENTS.md`, `STYLE_GUIDE.md`, `PR_GUIDELINES.md`, and `.github/pull_request_template.md`. Read nested `AGENTS.md` files applicable to every changed path. Resolve these from the target repository, not the skill's installation directory. If reviewing changes to the rules themselves, also inspect the base versions so removing a requirement cannot silently erase a finding.
3. Resolve the Linear ticket from an explicit identifier, then the PR or branch. Use the repository's `$scope-check` skill for the `Done When` boundary and its separate Scope check output. Missing ticket access or acceptance criteria blocks the scope conclusion, not independent standards checks.
4. Use command results and manual testing evidence tied to the reviewed revision. A checked box or successful unrelated CI job is not proof of all validation. Record the reviewed head and any local changes so stale evidence is identifiable.

## Evaluate adherence

- Inspect the complete diff and enough surrounding code to assess applicable TypeScript, UI, organization, comments, documentation, hygiene, and testing rules. Focus findings on introduced or modified code, not unrelated existing debt.
- Check title and branch conventions, ticket linkage, PR body requirements, size guidance, split justification, review entry points, testing evidence, Loom, and review/check status against `PR_GUIDELINES.md`.
- Distinguish mandatory rules from preferences. Words such as “prefer” and “ideally,” the 200-line target, and the five-file guideline need judgment. Above 400 changed lines, excluding tests, check for the required explanation and review guide rather than rejecting the size alone.
- Explain concerns briefly to the PR author so they can address them; formal rule citations and evidence for each finding are not required. Do not invent exceptions, team approval, testing outcomes, or video contents. If a required document is unavailable or rules conflict without a clear applicable resolution, report the gap instead of guessing.
- Respect workflow timing: missing Loom or review evidence can be reported as outstanding before requesting review while a draft is being prepared. Do not call future post-merge steps violations on an open PR.
- Keep scope expansions in Scope check. Verification is optional. Standards check only records whether the check ran.

## Return the result

Return a copy-ready section:

```markdown
## Standards check

- [x] Ran `$dg-pr-adherence-check` against the final diff and PR metadata.
```

The checkbox means the review ran, not that all requirements passed. If the diff cannot be resolved or the review could not run, leave it unchecked and tell the author what blocked it. Separately make any outstanding findings or unverified requirements known to the PR author so they can address them; do not require these details in the PR body. Rerun affected checks after changes to code, rules, or PR metadata.

content.text:
Verified both code-changing findings — and #6 is real. Here's the triage.

## One actual bug, worth fixing before merge

**The legacy config tree is no longer refreshed before reading block uids.** The deleted `GeneralSettings` did this:

```ts
const settings = useMemo(() => {
  refreshConfigTree();                 // ← dropped
  const tree = discourseConfigRef.tree;
```

The new `useLegacyConfigBlocks` hook skips the refresh, with a comment claiming every writer and the dialog's close already cover it. That misses the first open, and any edit made directly on the `[[discourse graph/config]]` page. If the tree is stale, the hook gets `uid: undefined` for a block that exists, and the panel creates a **second** `trigger` / `Canvas Page Format` / `(BETA) Left Sidebar` block. Duplicate legacy blocks mean readers pick one arbitrarily. That's precisely the class of silent-reset bug this PR is careful about everywhere else. Fix is restoring one line.

## Small mandatory fixes

- `DiscourseContextSettings.tsx` and `PreferencesStyling.tsx` still lack explicit return types — CodeRabbit's list named six components, and these two weren't on it.
- My comment in `settingsTabs.ts` says "every in-repo call site is updated". That's PR history, not a lasting constraint, so it fails the style guide's durable-comment rule.

## One that conflicts with your own preference — your call

The check flags **no unit tests for `resolveSettingsTabId` and the alias map** as mandatory, and it's a fair target: pure functions, and your own inline annotation says a wrong alias fails silently. But your saved preference is throwaway harnesses, not committed tests, and the stack has commits literally titled "Drop unit tests." I won't override that on a checklist's say-so.

## PR body — needs your OK to edit

- **Mandatory:** the ~1,000-line diff needs a split justification, review entry points, and a testing path in the Reviewer brief. The body also predates main's template: no `## Standards check`, the Loom isn't under its heading, and Verification sits inside a `<details>` so it doesn't render as a heading.
- **Now false:** the *Left sidebar placement* bullet (it says the toggle stays on the tab), the *New behaviour* placeholder bullet (reverted), "the enable toggle gates the left sidebar sections", and "142/142 tests" (it's 383).
- Two of your inline self-annotations are stale too — [GeneralSettings.tsx](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1373#discussion_r3895785239) names the wrong destination file and the wrong hook filename.

## What I couldn't verify

- **Scope vs. Done When** — Linear needs re-authorizing (`claude mcp` or your claude.ai connector settings), so the scope conclusion is blocked.
- **Roam manual testing** in the body predates the tab-hiding commit. Your new Loom may cover it; I can't watch videos.

Still unresolved from earlier: I couldn't find the red lint check you mentioned. A link or screenshot would settle it.

**The decision I need:** Michael approved today, on the current head. Pushing the refresh fix and the two return types will likely reset that approval and need him to look again. Do you want me to push those fixes now and re-request review, or merge as-is and put the refresh bug in a follow-up?
